passage:
Marta Sandoval spent thirty years compiling the first dictionary of the dialect of the high mountain province, working at a kitchen table between teaching posts. What happened to those finished pages is still argued about in the valleys she recorded. No volume of her own was ever bound, and she never paid a printer anything at all. The university library asked twice for the manuscript, and she had still not answered when the slips left for the capital; nothing reached the library. A newspaper offered to print one letter of the alphabet a month, and she refused to let the work appear in parts. A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name. A publisher across the border wanted a translation, but nothing of hers appeared abroad in any language.

One market day a week for nineteen years she stood among the stalls asking sellers what they called things, certain that people speak most truly while haggling over goods. She began each market day with the same question, the old name for a measure of oil, and set down whatever the first stall told her. A word went onto a card the first time a seller said it, without waiting for a second mouth. Parish books and wills she never opened, holding that a word owes nothing to having once been written down. The village teachers offered to have their classes write to her, and she refused: a child's page reaches the post already corrected. She kept no correspondents in other villages, saying that one market draws twelve villages to it, so postbags were waste.

Her name appears nowhere in his three volumes, not even among the thanks. It is no comedy, and hardly a waste, since the words did survive; her stubbornness is not the point, and impatience would be misplaced. The feeling the story leaves is indignation on her behalf, at a theft nobody has yet called one.

Ferrand has never thought of itself as a hot city, but for nine consecutive summers its public hospital has logged an August spike in patients treated for heat exhaustion. In 2021 the municipal health office, led by Dr. Mireille Okonjo, tried to interrupt the pattern with a pilot it called Open Doors. Six branch libraries were fitted out as cooling rooms, with chilled water, fans, and staff trained to recognize the early signs of heat illness. The rooms opened at dawn and stayed open until four in the afternoon, on the reasoning that the danger arrives during the working day. The office asked every construction and landscaping employer in the city to post the schedule at job sites, because the pilot was built around people who work outdoors, the group Okonjo believed least able to escape the afternoon heat.

The office had a way of checking whether Open Doors worked. Every heat-exhaustion case at the hospital is recorded with the patient's age, home district, and hour of arrival, and the records reach back far enough to build a nine-year baseline. Okonjo compared August 2021 against that baseline. Visits by people taken ill on outdoor jobs fell twelve percent below the nine-year average. The fall was not spread evenly: on the days the city issued no heat alert, worker visits matched the baseline exactly. The whole of the improvement was concentrated in the days alerts went out.

Okonjo was the first to say that the number is not yet an argument. That same summer, she pointed out, the city began sending heat alerts by text message, so the alerts and the rooms went out together and nothing in the records separates them. Until the two are pulled apart, she argued, nobody can say which of them produced the twelve percent. The council agreed with her and kept the alerts citywide while running cooling rooms in only three of the six branches, so that next August can tell the measures apart. Ferrand's August records will be read again next year, and this time the health office knows what it is looking for.

passage:
The mural on Rowan Street Station's west stair is called the last work of the painter Cecile Mabry. Five accounts of its making circulate: that Mabry painted it herself, that her apprentice Tomas Vane finished it, that three sign-painters worked from her drawing, that the rival Halloran of Preswick was paid for it, and that her brother Emile copied an earlier panel. The station's papers opened last year.

The papers put the brush in the sign-painters' hands. Three were hired from the goods yard, and her drawing issued to them. Mabry never mounted the scaffold, being at Ashe that winter. Vane drew no wages that winter, being at work in Leeds. Halloran of Preswick was paid nothing, and his ledger shows none. Emile signed nothing and appears only as a mourner.

The ground for doubting the old label is a supplier's letter, a reason nobody had. No undercoat lies beneath the paint; plaster took the colour. There is no soil behind that wall, which backs onto the ticket hall. Nothing there serves as a background; figures crowd the wall. Whoever painted it lacked training in drawing, as the hands show. The reopening photograph shows how the concourse was lit. The mural has taken no damage since, so the photograph shows none. The photograph is undated and fixes nothing about the work. No figure in that crowd can be identified. The crowd's reaction goes unrecorded; every face is turned away.

The next step is to look for the squared drawing copyists would have marked. The brushwork of her signed canvases settles nothing; she never touched it. Hunting the walls Vane painted later is idle. Halloran's letters at Preswick prove nothing about a wall he never saw. No earlier panel exists; the design was invented here.

The station's silence since then annoys me more than the finding. My agreement with it is not settled. No reluctance holds me back; I accept it. Curiosity is not what it leaves me. I have no sympathy for anyone it displaces.

Borrowing at the Fenn Street library doubled between 2016 and 2019, while every other branch in the borough lost readers. Five causes have been offered: the rerouted number nine bus; the closing of the Bourne Road branch; the longer evening hours; the ending of overdue fines; a new school reading requirement. The borough's own data settle it.

The school rule accounts for it: the rise is confined to readers of eleven to fourteen, and began the term the rule took effect. The daytime totals rose as fast, and evening borrowing was flat. The number nine has kept its old route for thirty years. Bourne Road is open still, and not one card came over. Fines are charged as they always were, and no debt was forgiven.

A figure crosses the window at closing, which is the caretaker on his round. No number is quoted here, and eleven thousand is nobody's total. Mrs Aidoo is unknown outside the branch and opens no doors. Staff reckon nothing by hand; a machine does the arithmetic. The report carries no diagram, and its pages hold only text.

A counter on the door has logged every entry since 2012. Its use is age: entries are tied to cards, so the eleven-to-fourteens are picked out. It keeps no clock, and its entries carry no hour. No postcode is attached to an entry, and no line appears. Bourne Road's entries are kept elsewhere and never added in. No account is matched to an entry, and debts stay invisible.

Another branch could repeat the rise only by having a school set reading for its pupils; nothing else on that list moved these figures. The borough has had three years to copy this and has not stirred. The staff have earned no particular praise, and I offer none. The branch was funded generously and wanted for nothing. The numbers are sound; I would not have them counted again. I do not leave the judging to others; my verdict is plain.

Port Alden sits at the mouth of a shallow bay, on a coast the Admiralty charts of the period marked simply as sand, shifting. A current runs along that coast from the west, carrying sand eastward past the town all winter. For most of the nineteenth century the fishing fleet lay at anchor in the open, and in a hard gale the boats were hauled up the beach by hand. In 1893, after two winters in which nine boats were lost, the borough appointed a harbour commission and gave it a single instruction: make the inner basin safe. The commission's engineer was Marguerite Hallam, then thirty-four, who had built two river locks and no sea works at all.

Hallam laid four schemes before the commissioners that autumn, and in December they adopted a stone mole, six hundred yards long, run out from the eastern headland to shelter the basin behind it. Work began in the spring of 1894 and was finished, at a cost of eleven thousand pounds, in the autumn of 1897. For three seasons it seemed to answer. Insurance rates for the Port Alden boats fell by a fifth, and the borough borrowed against the improvement to pave the fish quay.

The county inspection of 1901 ended that confidence. The surveyors found that the mole had done what any wall set across a sand-bearing current will do: the anchorage behind it had silted to four feet at low water, and the deepest berths were gone. From 1902 skippers who had wintered at Port Alden for thirty years began running instead for the deeper harbour at Wexham, eleven miles east, and landing their catch there. Port Alden's winter earnings fell by rather more than a third within four years, and the quay loan, secured on a trade that had moved away, was not cleared until 1926.

Hallam's method was, in the strict sense, conservative: she had done what the profession then held to be safe, and she had done it well. Her defence, when it came, rested on the two soundings of the bay that existed in 1893, one of them thirty years old, neither of them extending east of the headland. Hallam left the coast in 1903 and never took sea work again.

In a dry valley in the western United States, a small creek used to vanish every summer. By August, its bed was cracked mud, and the meadows around it turned brown.

Scientists thought beavers could help. But the creek had too little wood and too few deep pools for beavers to settle there. So the scientists pounded rows of wooden posts across the creek and wove willow branches between them. The posts slowed the water just enough to form small ponds.

Within a year, beavers moved in and began building real dams on top of the posts. The ponds behind the dams spread water out into the meadows. The soaked ground acted like a sponge, slowly letting water seep back into the creek for months. Now the creek flows even in late summer, and the meadows stay green.

Not everyone was pleased at first. Some ranchers worried that the ponds would flood nearby roads. The scientists chose spots away from the roads, and over time the complaints died down.

options.F1P6-Q1-D: Scientists set posts in the creek so beavers would move in. The beavers' dams held the water back in ponds, so the meadows filled up while the creek ran dry.

The gate at my aunt's nursery sticks in August, and she has never oiled it. I got there at seven, before the sprinklers, and shoved it open with my shoulder. I had come only to cover the shifts of the man who quit on her Friday. There was no wage in it, and no pane of mine to pay for. School had nothing to do with the day, and neither of us mentioned selling. A gravel path ran from the gate to the greenhouse door.

A card hung over the register on a loop of twine: NOTHING GREEN LEAVES HERE TO DIE. I had lettered it myself that morning, word for word as she dictated; the card was two hours old, she has never written one out in her life, she was not joking when she gave me the words, and she did not go against it once all day.

At nine a woman came in with a fig tree in a black pot, brown to the stem, and no receipt. She talked for a long while. Odile carried the brown fig into the greenhouse to nurse and told her to come back in autumn: no money out of the till, no second tree, no soil and no advice, and the woman went home with her hands empty. Nothing alive gets thrown out of this shop, she said. We had not grown that fig ourselves and it made no difference to her; a receipt has never decided anything here, and neither has a story from a stranger, and I am not teaching anybody a lesson.

I latched the gate at six. At breakfast I had told my mother exactly what my aunt would do, and I had been unkind and wrong about her. By evening the person I was ashamed of was myself. She had not been wrong about any of it, and I understood every step of what she had done. It was not admiration I felt, and there was nothing in the day to laugh at.

Every weekday for eleven weeks, Dr. Imani Rowe left unmarked envelopes on the paving stones of a busy transit plaza and waited to see what strangers would do. Each envelope held a blank card and nothing of value. A staffed lost-property kiosk stood about twenty metres away, and Rowe's team counted an envelope as returned only if it reached that counter within the hour. Field studies of this kind trade the tidiness of a laboratory for the messiness of real behaviour, and Rowe accepted the trade willingly. Across 1,200 drops, the plain envelopes came back 38 percent of the time.

Rowe's interest lay in a single change. On half of the drops, a first name and a short line of thanks were inked by hand across the envelope's corner, in what looked plainly like the loser's own handwriting. Under that condition returns climbed to 61 percent, a gap far larger than the weather, the hour, or the density of the crowd could account for. Rowe argued that the writing worked by making the loser particular: it is easy to step around an abstraction and hard to step around a person, and a name turns a dropped object into somebody's loss, even when the finder will never meet that somebody.

Dr. Tomas Vance, who studies pedestrian movement, was unconvinced. His objection was not that Rowe's numbers were wrong; he accepted every one of them. It was that writing on an envelope is also a signal about contents, since people label what matters to them, and that finders were answering an impression of worth rather than any particular person.

The two designed a joint follow-up for the next spring, nine hundred drops in the same plaza, arranged so that their explanations predicted different results. One arm kept the inked name. The other carried a stamped serial number and the words CONTAINS PAYMENT, impersonal but unmistakably about stakes. The stamped envelopes came back 62 percent of the time and the inked ones 61. Rowe published the revision herself and now calls the effect a judgement about worth.

Rowe has become careful with the word why. The plaza gave her a number that almost anyone could go and reproduce; what it never handed over, she says, was the reason underneath it.

passage: Microloans are small loans for people whom banks turn away. People once hoped these loans would lift families out of poverty by helping them start businesses. Careful studies have cooled that hope. Most borrowers did not earn more, and their businesses rarely grew past a very small size. But the studies agree on a quieter benefit. The loans helped families with the timing of their spending. Families could get through lean months and pay for big, one-time costs they could not have managed otherwise. Microloans, the evidence suggests, do not create new wealth. Instead, they help families spread the money they already have across time.

The bus set Iris down at the top of Tarn Row at four o'clock, and she walked the last hundred yards the way she had walked them at nine, counting the iron gates. There were still eleven. She had the clerk's letter folded in her coat, because a tin had been left for her in the coal shed - her name on the lid in a hand she did not know - and she had been written to twice to say it would be thrown out at the end of the month. Nobody could tell her what was in it.

The house was smaller than the house she had been carrying. Everyone had warned her about that, and it was true, and it cost her nothing. What cost her something was the railings. The iron was gone from the whole length of the row, both sides, and a low clipped hedge ran in its place, identical outside every house.

Mr. Halloway was in his doorway across the road, twenty years older all at once, and he knew her before she spoke. "You'll have seen," he said, and tipped his chin at the hedge. "We voted on it. You'd have had a paper if you'd left an address."

Iris began the sentence she had been assembling since the bus - that a street is not only the people who happen to sleep in it - and stopped in the middle of it. Halloway was not wrong. Eleven gates on the row, and she had not written to one of them in twenty years.

The tin was where the letter said, under a sack, lighter than she had expected. She opened it at the gate: one long key, for the back door that had been bricked up before she was born, and nothing else at all. She put it in her pocket, which was ridiculous, and at the corner she stopped and wrote her address on the back of the clerk's letter for Halloway.

In the villages below the Corran Ridge, people say that the dusk newts of Pellam Pond climb the ridge each October to see the first stars of winter. Grandparents tell children that a newt who reaches the crest before dawn will live a hundred years, and on damp autumn nights families still walk up with lamps to watch the small olive salamanders pass.

The biologist Mara Odell, who came to study the newts at the warden's request, preferred a plainer explanation. Her first guess was stale water, since rotting oak leaves can strip a pond of oxygen in autumn. An oxygen meter lowered to the bottom showed the water as fresh in October as in June.

She next wondered whether the newts were laying eggs on the ridge, but a search of its moss the following spring found almost none. So she fixed a visit from a soil scientist, who helped her bury small thermometers beneath the slope. Through the winter they told the story: the ridge's deep soil stayed above freezing while the floor of the pond grew bitterly cold, and the newts had burrowed down to spend the winter in its warmth.

The reserve had meant to regrade the ridge path that year with a small digger. The machine never came, and the path is left as it was, rutted and muddy, while the volunteers who once offered to rake the pond have found other work. A proposal to rope off the mossy slopes was set aside as well.

Odell's thermometers are surely right. Still, when I walked up the ridge last October and saw a grandmother crouched with her lamp, telling a boy to watch for the newt that would see the stars, I found myself missing the story I grew up with, and half wishing I had never read the data.

For six seasons Ines Marchetti followed grey chatterbirds through the thorn scrub of the eastern Karoo, and for six seasons one habit refused to make sense. Chatterbirds keep a piercing two-note call for hawks alone; when it sounds, every bird within earshot drops flat or dives into cover, and nobody forages for a minute or more. Yet Marchetti's notebooks filled with hawkless alarms — three hundred and forty of them, by her own count, with nothing overhead but cloud.

Her first thought was ordinary error: a shadow, a startled dove, a bird jumping at nothing. But mistakes ought to be scattered evenly through a group, and these were not. Sixty-nine percent of the hawkless calls came from whichever bird had taken the sentinel perch above the group, the one spot from which the whole foraging party can be watched, and a sentinel has the least excuse for mistaking a shadow.

What followed the calls was just as lopsided. Marchetti filmed fifty-eight hawkless alarms at close range. In forty-one of them the caller dropped from its perch within seconds and carried off the item a startled neighbour had let fall — usually something bulky: a scorpion, a hairless mouse, a beetle grub too fat to swallow whole.

Correlation is not proof, so in her fifth season Marchetti set out to make the alarms happen. On alternate mornings she baited the feeding stations either with slivers of meat that go down in a gulp or with whole scorpions, which a bird must beat and dismember in the open. Hawkless alarms were five times more common on scorpion mornings, and on those mornings the caller finished the meal.

Marchetti now calls the hawkless alarm a lie told for a mouthful: a signal meaning hawk, given by a bird that eats when everyone else believes it. What she cannot explain is why the lie still works. A hundred and forty liars a season ought to have taught the flock to ignore the call, and it has not. Whether the callers hold the trick below some rate at which listeners would stop believing it is the question she means to answer next.

When the Calder Street branch library in Redhaven reopened after its refit, the council expected a crowd. None came: the door counter recorded as many visitors as before. What changed was how long they stayed: visits of over an hour roughly doubled. Two sociologists, Ostrander and Njoku, spent two years finding out why.

Four changes could explain the pattern; three did not survive. The longer hours cannot explain it: the added time came in the evening, but the new visits end before six. The doorway now faces the market square, but the newcomers come from the streets behind and never make that walk. The refit cut eight enclosed rooms from the open floor, but their doors stayed shut and the hours are spent at the open tables. What remains is the rule at the door: the card check was dropped, and nearly every new long visitor carries no card.

Proving the change real meant settling an old question: the logbook's fourth column is headed Reserve, a word this town uses in four ways. In that heading it does not mean the duplicate volumes held back from the shelves; it does not mean the woodland reserve at the parish edge; it does not mean a room claimed in advance. It means the repair fund kept against the roof, a sum set aside year by year; the column recorded money, not readers.

Who stayed? Not home workers, who would come any weekday, when the rise stops in the school holidays. Not market shoppers, who would come on market days alone; the rise is even. Not the depot's early-shift workers, at their machines until six. The newcomers arrive together just after three, in term time only. The Fenwick branch, in the next town, entered because the local logbook counted money rather than readers: the earlier figures had to come from its unbroken records. It was not brought in to rule out a rival explanation, nor to show the pattern in a second town, nor to fix the limits of the claim. The counting was exact and the labour was not out of proportion, but the conclusion outruns the evidence, and nothing here is settled. The doubt is not how far the finding travels but whether it holds here.

passage:
The shop smelled of felt and hot glue, and I have not walked past an open piano since without checking, out of habit, whether the lid is propped at the angle Serrano preferred. I was fifteen when my mother left me at his door with a note saying only that I was willing. He read it twice, folded it into his apron pocket, and then did not speak to me about tuning for a long while.

For the first four months he sat me on a stool beneath the raised lid of whatever instrument he was working on, and had me count. Two strings of a unison, struck together, throb at a rate; I was to say the number of throbs in a second, aloud, and be corrected until I was right. I was not permitted to put a tool to a string.

I had come expecting hammers and wire. I had a picture of myself in it, too: the small tool, the held breath, the string coming true under my hand. Devlin, the other apprentice, who had arrived a season ahead of me, told me not to ask what any of it was for. I asked anyway, in February, when my patience gave out.

He said that a tuner is a witness before he is a workman, and that most of the damage done in the trade is done by men whose hands are quicker than their ears. "A doctor who cannot hear a heart," he said, "may still own a very fine stethoscope." What I had once heard, he said, I could not afterward pretend not to have heard.

Then he turned back to the instrument on the bench and left me to make of it what I could. I did not understand him that winter. I understood him, I think, on a Tuesday four years later, in a rented hall in Trentham, when a piano I had been given two hours to prepare went wrong under my hands and I found that I already knew what to do without deciding to know it.

Serrano died the spring before last. I have his bench now, and three apprentices of my own, and every one of them asks me in February the question I asked him.

What he gave me was not a technique but a way of waiting, and I have had to be careful since not to make a virtue of the waiting itself. I tell my three the truth: the counting is dull, and a season of it will cost them nothing they will miss. Then I put them under the lid and leave them there. Close listening is the whole of the trade; the lever only carries out what the ear has already settled.

passage:
My grandmother was the last jobbing printer on Ferris Street, and her shop closed the winter I turned nine. My family repeats five reasons: her failing eyesight, a rent the landlord doubled, her partner Ines leaving for Dunmore, a copy shop across the street, and a flood in the cellar that spoiled the paper. Last spring I read her ledgers.

The ledgers settle it: the landlord doubled the rent. March's entry is twice February's, and she asks what a press would fetch. Her eyesight held; she read register marks by lamplight that winter. Ines stood at the stone until the final week. The copy shop opened the spring after the doors shut. The cellar stayed dry, and the paper went on unspoiled.

That last night she set the handbill on the stone, deposited among the rest. No type was arranged; the cases stayed shut under cloths. No day was appointed, and the carter came when he pleased. The ink never hardened, though she washed the slab at ten. The sun had not descended; the chimneys were still bright. The ledger's last page corrects a guess of mine: I had put the closing a year early. No date stands there to fix the order of anything. Her handwriting is not on it; a bindery clerk kept the book. It shows nothing of how the work was priced. It names no others who worked there, only herself.

She needed a lease at a fixed rent, and the landlord signed none. Someone to read her proofs aloud she never needed. The bench beside her held a second printer trained already. Work no copier could match kept arriving all that winter. Her storeroom stood above the water and her reams stayed dry.

My admiration for how she closed the shop carries one regret: she might have told us. Unreserved my admiration is not, whatever the ledgers show. Her silence draws no criticism from me; she owed us nothing. Detachment is beyond me; the shop was my own family's. Nor does her stubbornness amuse me.

passage:
In the spring of 1802 the council of Kirrholm, a river town of about two thousand people, took up a question it had put off for eleven years: whether to replace the rope ferry across the Vess with a stone bridge. The ferry was old and cheap. The bridge would cost more than the town's whole yearly revenue, and the money would have to be borrowed from a banking house in Reval. The recorder, Petra Lund, left four pages of minutes that give the hour of adjournment and the tally but not the arguments; what the council actually weighed has had to be reconstructed from the letters its members wrote that summer.

In the ice-run of March 1801 the ferry rope had parted and three people drowned within sight of the town landing, and the memory of it sat in the chamber all spring. Lorens Falk, the engineer the council had hired in 1799, argued against the bridge, and argued from the same fact. Piers set in a channel that narrow would catch the floes each March, dam them, and push the water back over the lower streets. Safety, he told the members, was the reason to leave the river alone.

The chamber had been divided since 1791, and Falk's warning kept it divided. Twice the members split six and six, and twice Margit Aden, who held the chair and its casting vote, declined to use it and adjourned the session instead. On the third division the tally was six and six again. This time Aden cast, and cast for the bridge, saying only that the town could not be asked to wait through another winter for a crossing.

In March 1809 the floes piled against the piers exactly as Falk had said they would, and the water stood a foot deep in the lower streets for nine days. The town borrowed a second time and opened a fourth arch in 1814, after which the flooding stopped. The bridge Kirrholm wanted was the bridge Kirrholm got. The objection it had voted down was also correct, and the correction cost more in 1814 than it would have cost in 1802.

Lund's minutes preserve none of the arguing. They give the hour the council rose, half past eight, and the tally, and nothing more.

options.F1P16-Q1-A: Aden's decision, after twice declining and adjourning, to use the chair's casting vote on a third six-and-six division, which carried the measure by one.
options.F1P16-Q1-B: The switch of three ten-year opponents in the week the stone went to the Hallby quarry two of them owned, which carried it eight votes to four.
options.F1P16-Q1-C: Aden's proposal to service the Reval loan from bridge tolls rather than the hearth tax, which brought four long-standing opponents across and carried it seven to five.
options.F1P16-Q1-D: Aden's moving the division forward by a week while the two leading opponents were downriver, which carried it nine votes to none with three seats empty.
